title: How Exorcism Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss exorcism, opening with science fiction writer Philip K. Dick's belief that he was possessed by an alien intelligence that improved his life. They contrast spirit possession with psychological explanations, cover the Catholic Church's approach to exorcism (signs of possession, the Rite of Exorcism, holy water, relics, investigation and psychological evaluation, roughly one in five thousand cases), the International Association of Exorcists, the film The Exorcist, a sociologist's book on American exorcisms, and for-profit exorcism by Bob Larson Ministries. The episode closes with a listener correction about the Framingham Heart Study.

entities.name: American Exorcism: Expelling Demons in the Land of Plenty

segments.title: Opening and Philip K. Dick's alien possession
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the show, then discuss science fiction writer Philip K. Dick, who believed an alien intelligence had possessed him and improved his life.

segments.title: Spirit intrusion versus psychological disorders
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how beliefs in spirit intrusion differ across the world, and how conditions such as epilepsy, schizophrenia and dissociative identity disorder were once mistaken for possession. They raise the question of whether psychology and spirit possession describe the same thing.

segments.title: Psychological treatments and electroconvulsive therapy
segments.summary: The hosts note that psychology has its own methods for treating disturbances, including antidepressants, psychotherapy and electroconvulsive therapy, which is still used today.

segments.title: Catholic Church and signs of demonic possession
segments.summary: Chuck describes his Catholic upbringing and how the Church's exorcism practice seems rooted in mysticism. The hosts list the traditional signs of possession, including speaking in unlearned languages, knowing hidden things, superhuman strength, and aversion to religious images. Speaking in tongues is said to be considered an expression of religious ecstasy rather than a sign of possession.

segments.title: The Exorcist film and the Rite of Exorcism
segments.summary: The hosts compare the film The Exorcist with real Catholic exorcisms, saying the rite is a set of prayers with call and response, holy water, crucifixes and relics. They also mention saints' relics being distributed to churches.

segments.title: Church investigation and sociologist's account of exorcisms
segments.summary: A request for exorcism triggers an investigation, which may include a psychological evaluator and medical doctor; the hosts say about one in five thousand cases is deemed a real possession or worth an exorcism. They describe a sociologist's book on American exorcisms and a depressed man named Warren whose exorcism was anticlimactic.

segments.title: Shortage of exorcists, risks, and for-profit exorcism
segments.summary: The hosts explain the Church has few exorcists, with eleven priests and the International Association of Exorcists. They discuss the risk of harming people with treatable disorders and then describe Bob Larson's ministry, which stages exorcisms for ticketed audiences, and a testimonial from Autumn in Toledo, Ohio.

segments.title: Listener correction on Framingham Heart Study
segments.summary: Chuck's mispronunciation of the Framingham Heart Study as Farmington is corrected by listener Glenna Carpenter Rhodius, and the hosts invite feedback.
